opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most interesting challenges right now, because the technology is moving so fast. If you're building a product today, you have to design it for where the technology will be in maybe twelve or eighteen months, not just where it is now. Otherwise, by the time you've polished it, the underlying capabilities have moved on and your product feels dated, or worse, the model itself has just absorbed what your product did.

So there's this tension. On the research side, at the frontier, you're pushing the capabilities as hard as you can. On the product side, you want something stable, reliable, and delightful for people to use every day. Those two cultures don't always naturally fit together. Part of what we've been trying to do is bring them much closer, so the product teams are almost co-designing with the researchers and can take advantage of new capabilities the moment they're ready.

The other thing I'd say is that I've always believed the best products come from the technology being almost invisible. Going back to my games design days, the goal wasn't to show off the AI. The AI was there to make the experience richer and more personal, to respond to what the player did. I think that's still the right lens. People don't want to think about the model or the parameters. They want something that understands their context, helps them get things done, and maybe surprises them in a good way.

And then you have to be thoughtful about responsibility. These are very powerful systems going out to billions of people, so you want to be bold about what's possible but careful and scientific about deployment: testing, understanding failure modes, and getting feedback from real use. Done well, the product becomes part of the scientific process. It tells you things about the technology you'd never learn in the lab.

r001.rationale: The response describes making technology invisible and creating experiences that feel richer, more personal, and helpful, but it does not identify imagining what product use would feel like as a design skill.

r002.rationale: It describes product teams co-designing with researchers and says product use feeds back into scientific learning, presenting product design and research as closely connected parts of an ongoing process.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that I've always seen the science and the products as deeply intertwined, not as separate activities. When we started DeepMind, the idea was that if you build general-purpose learning systems, they should be able to do many things, and products are really just a way of testing whether that's true. If your technology only works in the lab, on a benchmark, you haven't really understood it yet. Contact with real users, with messy real-world problems, that's where you find out what's actually missing.

So the way I think about it is that you want the frontier research and the product to form a kind of flywheel. The research produces capabilities that nobody has had before, and then the product work tells you what people actually need, what breaks, where the models are unreliable, and that feeds back into the research agenda. Some of the most important research problems we work on now, things like factuality, long-horizon planning, memory, tool use, these came into focus partly because we tried to put systems in front of people and saw where they fell short.

The hard part, and this is where I think a lot of people go wrong, is timing. With cutting-edge technology the capability curve is moving very fast, so you can't design a product for what the model can do today. You have to design for where it will be in six months or a year, otherwise by the time you ship, it's obsolete. But you also can't get too far ahead, because then you're building on capabilities that don't exist yet and the experience just doesn't work. So there's a kind of judgment, almost an intuition, about what's going to become robust soon, and that's something I spend a lot of time on.

The other principle I care about a lot is that the technology should be in service of people, it should be genuinely useful and it should earn trust. With something like AI, which is going to be so impactful, I think you have to be more careful than with a normal consumer product, not less. So we think hard about responsibility, about safety, about what should and shouldn't be built, and I actually think that's good product design too. The systems that people will rely on over the long term are the ones they can trust.

And finally I'd say the thing I find most exciting is that we're now at a point where the same underlying technology can help a scientist fold a protein, help a student learn something, and help someone plan their day. That universality is the whole point of AGI. So when we design products, I'm always asking whether this is bringing us closer to that vision of a system that can really understand and help with almost anything, rather than just a clever feature.

r001.rationale: The response discusses timing, usefulness, trust, and real-world product feedback, but does not identify imagining what using a product would feel like as a design skill.

r002.rationale: It describes science and products as “deeply intertwined” and says research and product work form a flywheel, with each informing the other.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with what you want to make possible for the person using it. With cutting-edge technology, it’s very tempting to get excited about the technology itself. But a demonstration that makes people say “wow” isn’t necessarily a useful product.

There are really two things you’re trying to understand: what can this technology do that wasn’t possible before, and where does that meet a real human need? You need to explore both. Sometimes the capability suggests an entirely new experience that people wouldn’t have known to ask for.

Then the design has to make that capability accessible. The underlying system might be enormously complex, but the interaction should feel intuitive. And with AI, that includes helping people understand when they can trust it and when they should check its work. That’s part of the product design, too.

So I’d build something, put it in people’s hands, and watch very carefully. Do they actually find it useful? Where does it frustrate them? That feedback is what turns an exciting technical possibility into something people want in their lives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human needs, new experiences, and intuitive interactions, but does not clearly identify imagining what using the product would feel like as a design skill.

r002.rationale: It describes building a product, observing people use it, and using their feedback to shape it, presenting design and user research as a connected process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the problem you’re trying to solve for someone. It’s very tempting, especially when you’ve got an exciting new technology, to build something that demonstrates the technology beautifully but doesn’t actually fit into anybody’s life.

At the same time, you can’t just ask people what they want, because they may not know what’s become possible. So there’s this interplay between understanding the technology deeply and understanding the user deeply. You build a prototype, put it in people’s hands, and learn where your assumptions were wrong.

And often the best product makes an enormous amount of complexity feel simple. The user shouldn’t need to understand the underlying machinery to get something useful out of it. But with AI, that simplicity also has to include being clear about its limitations, so people understand when they can rely on it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding users and testing prototypes, but does not clearly identify imagining what using the product would feel like as a design skill.
